passages.t: Judah's sons, and a widow wronged
passages.happening:
“About that time, Judah left his brothers and settled near a man named Hirah, an Adullamite” (verse 1). He marries a Canaanite woman, the daughter of Shua, and they have three sons: Er, Onan and Shelah (verses 2-5).

Judah gets a wife for Er, his eldest. “Her name was Tamar” (verse 6). “But Er, Judah's firstborn, was wicked in the sight of the LORD; so the LORD put him to death” (verse 7).

Judah tells his second son, “Sleep with your brother's wife. Perform your duty as her brother-in-law and raise up offspring for your brother” (verse 8).

“But Onan knew that the offspring would not belong to him; so whenever he would sleep with his brother's wife, he would spill his seed on the ground so that he would not produce offspring for his brother” (verse 9). “What he did was wicked in the sight of the LORD, so He put Onan to death as well” (verse 10).

Judah tells Tamar to live as a widow in her father's house until Shelah grows up. “For he thought, ‘He may die too, like his brothers’” (verse 11).
passages.hearers:
The story of Joseph has just begun, and suddenly Genesis turns to Judah. It can feel like an interruption. It is not. Judah is the brother who said, ‘What profit?’ and sold Joseph (37:26-27). This chapter shows him at his worst, so that we will see how far he changes later.

We are not told what Er's wickedness was. We are only told that God judged it.

Then comes a custom called levirate marriage. The name comes from the Latin word levir, ‘a husband's brother’. When a man died without a son, his brother married the widow. The first son born was counted as the dead man's son. He carried on the dead man's name and inherited his share of the family land. Israel's later law set out this duty (Deuteronomy 25:5-10). Law collections from the Hittites and from Assyria, Israel's ancient neighbors, also have rules of this kind. For a childless widow it was her security and her place in the family.

Now look at Onan. He takes Tamar as a wife, but he makes sure she never conceives. Why? If Tamar had a son, that son would inherit Er's share. If she had none, more would come to Onan. So he uses her and denies her what the custom was for. He takes the privilege and refuses the duty, again and again. The text calls it wicked.

Then Judah does wrong too. He blames Tamar for his sons' deaths, though the text says God judged them for their own wickedness. He sends her back to her father with a promise he does not mean to keep. She is left bound to Judah's family, with no husband and no child, and no way out.
passages.later:
Israel's law describes the duty Onan refused: “The first son she bears will carry on the name of the dead brother, so that his name will not be blotted out from Israel” (Deuteronomy 25:6).

The book of Ruth shows a wider form of the same care for a widow. Boaz marries Ruth “to raise up the name of the deceased through his inheritance” (Ruth 4:10). Jesus was once asked a question built on this law (Matthew 22:24-28).
passages.hard:
What exactly was Onan's sin? Christians have read verses 9-10 in more than one way.

Catholic teaching has long read the passage as condemning the act itself, as a way of preventing a child. Augustine read it that way, and Pope Pius XI cited his reading in the letter Casti Connubii (1930). Martin Luther and John Calvin also condemned the act itself. Those who hold this reading point out that Judah and Shelah also failed in the duty, yet only Onan was put to death.

Many Protestants today, and many scholars, read the sin as Onan's refusal of his duty to his brother's widow, while he used her for himself. They point out that verse 9 gives his motive in so many words: ‘so that he would not produce offspring for his brother.’

These notes take no side between these readings. On both, Onan wronged Tamar. He denied a widow her right and her future, for his own gain.
passages.asks: Onan took what he wanted from the custom and refused what it asked of him. Ask where you take the good of a relationship and refuse its cost. Then ask who is left waiting because of it.

passages.happening:
After a long time Judah's wife dies. When he has finished mourning, he goes up to Timnah where his sheep are being sheared (verse 12).

Tamar is told. “For she saw that although Shelah had grown up, she had not been given to him as a wife” (verse 14). She takes off her widow's clothes, covers her face with a veil, and sits by the road to Timnah (verse 14).

Judah sees her and thinks she is a prostitute (verse 15). He does not know she is his daughter-in-law. He asks to sleep with her. She asks what he will pay. He promises a young goat. She asks for a pledge until it comes: “Your seal and your cord, and the staff in your hand” (verse 18). He gives them, sleeps with her, and she becomes pregnant (verse 18).

She goes home, takes off the veil, and puts her widow's clothes back on (verse 19).
passages.hearers:
Tamar has waited for years. Shelah has grown up. No one has come. Judah has broken his word, and she has no court to take him to. In that world a widow in her position could not simply marry someone else; she was still bound to Judah's family.

So she acts. The text tells it briefly and plainly. She disguises herself, and Judah, a widower on his way to a feast, takes her for a prostitute and uses her. Sheep-shearing was a time of feasting and celebration.

Tamar is shrewd. She asks for a pledge, something to hold until the payment comes. And she asks for the three things that prove who he is. A seal was a small carved stone with its owner's own mark, used to sign by pressing it into clay. It hung on a cord. A staff could carry its owner's marks too. Together they were like a signature and an identity card. Tamar is not after the goat. She is after proof.

Notice the clothing. She takes off her widow's clothes, then puts them back on. The story turns on clothes and disguise, as the last chapter did. Judah once helped deceive his father with Joseph's robe and a young goat. Now he himself is deceived, and a young goat is again the price.
passages.later:
Israel's later law forbids a man to sleep with his daughter-in-law: “You must not have sexual relations with your daughter-in-law” (Leviticus 18:15). Genesis does not hide that this is what happened.

Another widow, Ruth, also takes a bold step at night to claim her right: “Spread the corner of your garment over me, for you are a kinsman-redeemer” (Ruth 3:9). Ruth is honorable where Judah was not, and Boaz acts rightly where Judah did not.
passages.asks: Tamar was wronged by the man who should have looked after her, and she had no one to take her case to. Ask who in your world is left without a voice or a court. Then ask whether you are the person who could speak for them.

passages.happening:
Judah sends his friend Hirah with the young goat to get his pledge back. Hirah cannot find the woman. The men of the place say, “No shrine prostitute has been here” (verse 21). “Let her keep the items,” Judah replies. “Otherwise we will become a laughingstock” (verse 23).

About three months later Judah is told, “Your daughter-in-law Tamar has prostituted herself, and now she is pregnant” (verse 24). “Bring her out!” Judah replies. “Let her be burned to death!” (verse 24).

As she is brought out, Tamar sends word: “I am pregnant by the man to whom these items belong.” “Please examine them. Whose seal and cord and staff are these?” (verse 25).

“Judah recognized the items and said, ‘She is more righteous than I, since I did not give her to my son Shelah.’ And he did not have relations with her again” (verse 26).
passages.hearers:
Judah is worried about one thing: being laughed at. He would rather lose his seal than lose face.

Hirah uses a different word for the woman than Judah did. Judah thought she was a prostitute. Hirah asks for a ‘shrine prostitute’, a different Hebrew word. Scholars debate what that word meant. Older scholars thought prostitution at shrines was common in Canaan. Many now say the evidence for it is unclear.

Then the double standard. Judah slept with a woman he took for a prostitute, and thought nothing of it. When he hears that Tamar is pregnant, he orders her burned to death. As head of the family he claims the right to judge her. The same act is nothing for him and death for her.

Tamar does not accuse him in public. She sends the items quietly and says, ‘Please examine them.’ Those are almost the very words Judah and his brothers used when they sent Jacob the bloody robe: ‘Examine it’ (37:32). Now Judah is the one who must look and recognize.

And he does. ‘She is more righteous than I.’ It is the turning point of Judah's life in Genesis. He does not excuse himself. He names his wrong: I did not give her to my son. ‘More righteous’ does not mean every step of her plan was good. It means that between the two of them she was in the right. She kept faith with the family's duty, and he did not.

This is the first time in Genesis that one of Jacob's sons admits he was wrong.
passages.later:
Judah's change carries on. Later, when Benjamin is about to be made a slave in Egypt, it is Judah who offers himself instead: “please let your servant stay here as my lord's slave in place of the boy” (Genesis 44:33).

Jesus spoke of the same double standard: “Why do you look at the speck in your brother's eye, but fail to notice the beam in your own eye?” (Matthew 7:3). When a crowd brought him a woman to be stoned, and not the man, he said, “Let him who is without sin among you be the first to cast a stone at her” (John 8:7).
passages.asks: Judah was ready to burn Tamar for what he himself had done. Ask where you judge others harshly for things you excuse in yourself. Then ask whether you could say, as Judah did, ‘They are more in the right than I am.’

passages.happening:
Tamar gives birth to twins (verse 27). One puts out his hand first, and the midwife ties a scarlet thread around his wrist. “This one came out first,” she says (verse 28).

But he pulls his hand back, and his brother comes out first. “You have broken out first!” she says. “So he was named Perez” (verse 29). Then the brother with the scarlet thread is born, “and he was named Zerah” (verse 30).
passages.hearers:
Twins again, and a struggle at birth again, as with Jacob and Esau (25:24-26). The firstborn place goes to the one no one expected. Genesis keeps turning birth order upside down.

Perez means ‘breaking through’. Zerah may mean ‘rising’ or ‘shining’, like the dawn.

This chapter began with Judah leaving his brothers and losing two sons. It ends with two sons born. Tamar gets what was taken from her: children, a place in the family, and a future.

And the line runs on. Perez will be the ancestor of Boaz, and Boaz of King David. The family God chose to carry his promise is not a family of saints. It comes through a widow wronged and a man who learned, too late, that she was more righteous than he was.
passages.later:
The book of Ruth ends with Perez's family line: “Now these are the generations of Perez” (Ruth 4:18), running to Boaz and then to David (Ruth 4:21-22). The people bless Boaz, “may your house become like the house of Perez, whom Tamar bore to Judah” (Ruth 4:12).

Matthew's list of the ancestors of Jesus names only a few women, and Tamar is the first: “Judah was the father of Perez and Zerah by Tamar” (Matthew 1:3). Matthew does not say why. Many readers think he wanted us to see that God's mercy works through people the world looked down on.
passages.asks: God brought the line of David, and of Jesus, through this broken family. Ask whether you think your family's story is too broken for God to use. Then ask whether Tamar's place in Matthew 1 changes your answer.
